rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human beings are distinguished from other creatures by speech, which lets them articulate and comprehend, as well as by knowing revelation.
rows.anchor: they distinguished from all other creatures by the faculty of speech through which they both articulate and comprehend

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Verses 2–4 can allude to God's honoring humanity by enabling people to learn and recite the Quran, His Word, as in 44:58 and 54:17, 22, 32, and 40.
rows.anchor: allusion to God’s honoring human beings by making the Quran, His very Word, something they are capable of learning and reciting (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayān means speech and also something clear or evident.
rows.anchor: Speech translates bayān, which also means something that is clear or evident.

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some understand bayān as alluding to God's teaching Adam all the names, as in 2:31.
rows.anchor: seen by some as an allusion to God’s having taught Adam the names, all of them (2:31; see 2:31c)

rows.speaker: Q, Sh
rows.claim: Another proposed sense is God's teaching people to distinguish good from evil, permitted from forbidden, and truth from falsehood through revelation.
rows.anchor: distinguish between good and evil, between what is permitted and what is forbidden (Q, Sh) or between truth and falsehood

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Bayān is also regarded as a name of the Quran, as in 3:138, which calls it an exposition for humankind.
rows.anchor: Bayān is also considered one of the names of the Quran (Q, R), as in 3:138

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse depicts all celestial and earthly entities prostrating in submission to God, as in 22:18 and 16:49.
rows.anchor: this verse alludes to the prostration before God of all celestial and earthly entities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although najm is singular, it is understood collectively to mean all stars.
rows.anchor: Stars translates najm, which occurs in the singular, but is understood as a reference to all stars.

rows.speaker: Aj, Ṭ
rows.claim: Najm may instead mean herbs or all soft-stemmed plants, contrasted with trees as hard-stemmed plants.
rows.anchor: Najm could also be translated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether najm means stars or herbs, their prostration signifies complete submission to God's Will.
rows.anchor: In either interpretation, their prostration is an indication of their complete submission to God’s Will.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse parallels 28:78 and 77:35–36: the guilty are not questioned and cannot speak or make excuses; their deeds are already recorded, as in 17:71, 18:49, 50:17–18, 69:19–28, and 82:11–12.
rows.anchor: None shall be questioned that day, since their deeds have already been recorded

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that Day people cannot speak for themselves: mouths are sealed, hands and feet testify to deeds, and ears, eyes, and skins testify against them, as in 36:65 and 41:20.
rows.anchor: Their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to that which they used to earn (36:65)

rows.speaker: Aj, IK
rows.claim: Some reconcile this verse with 15:92–93 by saying people will first be questioned and then have their mouths sealed.
rows.anchor: some say that they will be questioned, and then their mouths will be sealed (Aj, IK)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Another explanation is that questioning is rhetorical reproach, not an attempt to elicit an answer.
rows.anchor: they will not be questioned in order to elicit a response, but only rhetorically, as a form of reproach (Aj)

rows.speaker: Sufi perspective
rows.claim: After the lower self is effaced through annihilation and subsistence in God, no sin remains because one can only act according to God's Will.
rows.anchor: when the attributes of the lower self have been effaced, after one has passed through the stations of both annihilation and subsistence in God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening phrase may be an adverbial clause modifying verse 39: they are not questioned because their marks already identify them.
rows.anchor: can also be read as an adverbial clause modifying v. 39, meaning that they will not be asked about their sins

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The guilty are contrasted with believers, whose signs include light on the body parts washed in ablution or the mark of prostration mentioned in 48:29.
rows.anchor: the marks by which the believers will be known, such as the light that shines from the parts of their bodies they washed when performing ablutions (IK)

rows.speaker: IK, Q
rows.claim: One interpretation is that the guilty are bent down and bound by their heads to their feet.
rows.anchor: their heads will be bent down and bound to their feet (IK, Q)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that angels drag the guilty by the forelock or by the feet.
rows.anchor: the angels will drag them by the forelock or by the feet (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran elsewhere says every crawling creature is held by God by its forelock, at 11:56.
rows.anchor: there is no creature that crawls, but that He holds it by its forelock (11:56)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With a full stop after verse 1, idhā introduces an event too terrifying to state directly.
rows.anchor: When v. 1 is read with a full stop at the end

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Read continuously with verse 2, idhā forms an adverbial clause: when the Event occurs, none can deny its occurrence.
rows.anchor: If it is read continuously with v. 2, it is considered an adverbial clause

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse may refer back to the previous sūrah: its promised blessings for the companions of the right and the foremost arrive when the Event befalls.
rows.anchor: a reference to the previous sūrah, meaning that all of the blessings promised to the companions of the right and to the foremost

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In either reading, the Event is the eschatological end of the world leading to the Day of Judgment.
rows.anchor: the Event refers to the eschatological event of the end of the world leading to the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-wāqiʿah derives from waqaʿa, to fall, happen, or occur, expressing inevitability: what must happen will happen.
rows.anchor: expresses a sense of inevitability

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The Event overwhelms deniers so that none who denied it in life can deny it any longer.
rows.anchor: It will be so overwhelming that none of those who denied it in this life will be able to deny it any longer (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Event can also allude to an individual's transformation through sudden or profound spiritual realization.
rows.anchor: These verses can also be seen as an allusion to individual transformation through sudden or profound spiritual realization.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-sābiqūn comes from sabaqa, meaning to go first, go ahead, outstrip, or win a race.
rows.anchor: The foremost translates al-sābiqūn, which derives from the verb sabaqa

rows.speaker: Aj, Z
rows.claim: Repeating the same word as subject and complement expresses something great and universally known.
rows.anchor: the same word is the subject and the complement, is used to express something that is great and known to all (Aj, Z)

rows.speaker: Many commentators
rows.claim: Many identify the foremost as the community's spiritual elite, who understand religion's inner meaning and walk toward God in this life.
rows.anchor: Many identify them with the spiritual elite of the community, who understand the inner meaning of the religion and walk toward God in this life.

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the foremost as the prophets.
rows.anchor: Most commentators consider the foremost to be the prophets (IK, JJ)

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: Some include saints, the truthful, and martyrs with the prophets because they outstrip others in faith.
rows.anchor: Some include the saints, the truthful

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Others hold that the prophets are beyond the foremost.
rows.anchor: while others believe the prophets to be beyond the foremost (Aj)

rows.speaker: Aj, IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: Other interpretations identify them as the first to accept Islam.
rows.anchor: Other interpretations include: the first to accept Islam (Aj, IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies them as the first members of the religious community, or ummah.
rows.anchor: the first members of the religious community

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They may be the sincere, foremost in answering God's call and sacrificing in pursuit of His Contentment.
rows.anchor: who are foremost in responding to the

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: They may be the first to come to the mosque and the first to set out in God's way.
rows.anchor: the first to come to the mosque, and the first to set out in the way of God (IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Another view identifies them as those foremost in attaining virtue.
rows.anchor: those who are foremost in attaining virtue (Aj)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Some interpret the foremost as residents of the highest parts of Heaven, associated with 83:18.
rows.anchor: the residents of the highest parts of Heaven (see 83:18; IK)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Some say the foremost bypass Reckoning and go directly to Paradise, while the companions of the left and right stand for judgment.
rows.anchor: the foremost will not be subject to the Reckoning before God on the Day of Judgment, going straight to Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes the foremost as brought nigh in Gardens of bliss.
rows.anchor: These verses could mean that the foremost are

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Another view says they are brought nigh to the Divine Throne.
rows.anchor: brought nigh to the Divine Throne (Z)

rows.speaker: Aj, JJ
rows.claim: Another view says they are brought nigh unto God Himself.
rows.anchor: brought nigh unto God Himself (Aj, JJ)

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAjībah says the brought-nigh were more numerous in earlier times, not greater in quality.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAjībah notes that the ones brought nigh were greater in earlier times with regard to quantity, not quality.

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some consider people near the end of time higher in degree because they awaken amid heedlessness and strive amid lassitude, earning a rank unavailable to others despite lacking earlier supports.
rows.anchor: Those toward the end of time are considered by some to be of a higher degree, because they have awakened in a time of heedlessness and exerted themselves in a time of lassitude.

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet tells his Companions that in their time omitting one tenth of what is commanded brings ruin, whereas later fulfilling one tenth brings salvation; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: the Prophet said to his Companions

rows.speaker: IK, JJ, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some identify the earlier group as previous religious communities and the later group as the Muslim community.
rows.anchor: Some maintain that those of old means earlier religious communities and those of later times means the Muslim community (IK, JJ, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Others interpret the earlier and later groups as earlier and later generations of Muslims.
rows.anchor: Others interpret them as references to earlier and later generations of Muslims (Z)

rows.speaker: ḥadīth
rows.claim: A famous hadith ranks the Prophet's generation first, followed by the two generations after it; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: The best generation is mine, then those who follow them, then those who follow them

rows.speaker: ḥadīth
rows.claim: A hadith describes a group in the Prophet's community that keeps following truth until the Hour, unharmed by those who fail to support or oppose it; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: A group among my community ceases not to follow the truth

rows.speaker: ḥadīth
rows.claim: A hadith describes later times as ruled by rapacity, obeyed passions, worldly priority, and each person's admiration of their own opinion; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: a ḥadīth states that at this time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These readings portray increasing spiritual devolution over time rather than human progress.
rows.anchor: these verses point to an ever greater spiritual devolution of human beings rather than progress over time

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The Noble Quran may refer to what has been discussed in this sūrah or to the Quran as a whole.
rows.anchor: a reference to everything that has been mentioned thus far in this sūrah or to the whole of the Quran (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quran here may carry its linguistic sense of a noble recitation.
rows.anchor: In this instance, Quran may be read according to its linguistic meaning

rows.speaker: R, Sh
rows.claim: Karīm indicates the combination of all praiseworthy attributes.
rows.anchor: Noble translates karīm, which indicates the joining together of all praiseworthy attributes (R, Sh).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What is noble is said to have pure origin and manifest bounty.
rows.anchor: is said to be of pure origin

rows.speaker: Aj, Q, R, Sh, Ṭ
rows.claim: Most take the concealed Book as the Preserved Tablet, said to contain every revealed book; 85:22 is cited.
rows.anchor: Book is taken by most to mean the Preserved Tablet (85:22; Aj, Q, R, Sh, Ṭ), which is said to contain all of the books of revelation.

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The Quran's nobility and concealment signify its preservation from influence by anyone but God, refuting claims that it is jinn's whispering or ancient fables; the commentary cites 6:25, 8:31, 16:24, 23:83, 25:5, 27:68, 46:17, 68:15, and 83:13.
rows.anchor: That it is both noble and concealed indicates that the Quran is preserved from the influence of anyone but God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Incredulity that God would send human messengers is a recurring barrier to belief, documented at 17:94 and many other verses.
rows.anchor: one of the constant barriers to belief, as in 17:94

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same human-messenger objection was made against Muhammad's prophethood, as in 25:7.
rows.anchor: This same objection is attributed to those who rejected the prophethood of Muhammad

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: God's Self-Sufficiency may mean He has no need of people or their belief and, though able, did not compel them to believe.
rows.anchor: could indicate that God has no need of them or no need for them to believe in Him; thus He did not compel them to believe in Him despite His ability to do so (R, Z)

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: God's being Praised is intrinsic to the Divine Nature and does not depend on anyone praising Him; the epithet often accompanies Self-Sufficiency, as in 4:131, 14:8, 22:64, 31:12, 31:26, 35:15, and 60:6.
rows.anchor: being praised is intrinsic to the Divine Nature and not dependent upon anything to praise Him (Āl)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Taḥrīm likely dates to 7/629 and is Madinan; a minority considers only verses 1–9 Madinan and the last three Makkan.
rows.anchor: al-Taḥrīm is a Madinan sūrah

rows.speaker: Āl, Suyūṭī
rows.claim: The sūrah is named al-Taḥrīm from its opening verse; other names are Limā tuḥarrimu, al-Mutaḥḥaram, and Sūrat al-Nabī, reflecting its address to the Prophet and his family situation.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the opening verse, in which the Prophet is told not to forbid for himself what God has permitted for him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah moves from the Prophet's relationship with his wives in verses 1–5 to believers' protection and repentance (6, 8), disbelievers' fate (7), and the Prophet's struggle against revelation's opponents (9).
rows.anchor: the subject of this sūrah is the relationship between the Prophet and his wives (vv. 1–5)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The examples of believing and disbelieving women show that everyone, including the Prophet's wives, is responsible for their own soul.
rows.anchor: it demonstrates that everyone, even the wives of the Prophet, is responsible for the state of his or her own soul

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Taḥrīm complements al-Mumtaḥanah, whose last verses emphasize women's own pledge to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: it complements Sūrah 60, al-Mumtaḥanah, the last verses of which emphasize the manner in which women made their own pledge with the Prophet

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Shielding oneself and one's family from the Fire means obedience and reverence to God, and enjoining them on one's family.
rows.anchor: Shield yourselves and your families by being obedient and reverent and enjoining obedience and reverence to God (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the only verse that tells believers to shield themselves from the Fire; elsewhere they ask God to protect them, as in 3:16, 3:191, and 40:7.
rows.anchor: This is the only verse in which believers are told to shield themselves from the Fire

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Stones likely refer to idols worshipped by idolaters because they were made of stone, or to stones themselves.
rows.anchor: stones likely refers to the idols worshipped by the idolaters, as they were made of stone (JJ) or were in fact stones

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels are guardians of Hell, whose number is given as nineteen in 74:30.
rows.anchor: The angels referred to here are the guardians of Hell, of whom the Quran says there are nineteen (74:30).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nūn is the Arabic letter n and a separated letter whose outward meaning is unspecified; many say its meaning is known only to God.
rows.anchor: whose meaning is not specified outwardly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the earliest sūrah in revelation chronology in which separated letters appear.
rows.anchor: This is the earliest sūrah in the chronological order of revelation in which the separated letters appear.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Nūn also means fish; some commentators connect it with an old Arab myth that Earth rests on a mythical fish's back.
rows.anchor: some commentators thus relate it to an old Arab myth

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others take Nūn's cup-shaped Arabic form as an allusion to the inkwell from which the pen draws ink.
rows.anchor: others say it refers to the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Islamic metaphysics, the Pen symbolizes the Divine Intellect or Logos through which God brings all things into being.
rows.anchor: In Islamic metaphysics, the Pen is often taken as a symbol for the Divine Intellect or Logos, through which God brought all things into being.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What the Pen writes signifies the existence of beings in creation, while Nūn represents the reservoir of possibilities manifested there.
rows.anchor: by the Pen then means existiation of beings in the created order

rows.speaker: ḥadīth qudsī
rows.claim: A famous hadith qudsi says God created the Pen first and commanded it to write the decree of all that would occur until the Hour; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: a famous ḥadīth qudsī states

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nūn may allude to Divine Names containing nūn: al-Raḥmān, al-Nūr, or al-Nāṣir.
rows.anchor: at the beginning of al-Nūr

rows.speaker: Bg, Q
rows.claim: Others connect Nūn with God's helping the believers, naṣr al-muʾminīn, a phrase appearing in 30:47.
rows.anchor: Others see it as a reference to God’s helping the believers (naṣr al-muʾminīn; Bg, Q)

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: Some attribute to the Prophet the saying that Nūn is a tablet of light; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: Some attribute to the Prophet the saying

rows.speaker: Bg, IK, JJ, Q
rows.claim: The pronoun they in that which they inscribe may refer to angels who record all human deeds; related passages include 43:80, 50:17–18, 80:15–16, 82:10–12, and 86:4.
rows.anchor: The pronoun they in that which they inscribe may be seen as a reference to the angels who record all human deeds

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī divides pens into those recording the decree until Resurrection, angels' pens recording human deeds, and human writing pens; he cites 18:49 for the second kind.
rows.anchor: According to al-Qurṭubī, pens are of three principal types
